newsitem.title: INDIA: India plays down hopes of large economic package.
newsitem.headline: India plays down hopes of large economic package.

text.p: The Indian government on Wednesday played down expectations that a large package of measures to spur financial markets would be announced this week, saying its efforts were more broadly focused.

A government spokesman was asked if New Delhi, as widely expected in the financial capital Bombay, would announce a large package of measures this week to shore up the capital markets where stocks and bonds are traded.
"The capital market is an important segment. The government effort is to move on a very broad front so the economy picks up in all sectors, not just the capital market," he told Reuters by telephone.

Other government officials said the financial markets may have become overly optimistic that the federal government would unveil a single package of measures by the end of the month to strengthen investors' confidence.

Expectations were first whetted in late December when Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda told industrialists his government planned steps by mid-January to shore up the capital market and boost economic growth.
The target date was later put off until January-end.

On Monday, Deve Gowda said the government would announce new economic policy measures this week before he and Finance Minister P. Chidambaram leave to attend the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland on January 31.

Deve Gowda's promises have helped to push up share prices at the Bombay Stock Exchange, where the benchmark 30-share index has risen about 17 percent this year and some 33 percent since hitting a three-year low of 2,713 points on December 4, 1996.
In afternoon trading on Wednesday, the index was up 5.51 points, or 0.15 percent, to 3,609.71.
"We are not expecting a mega-package," said a government official who asked not to be identified.

Earlier on Wednesday, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) said the stock market regulator was due to hold a board meeting on Thursday in the financial capital Bombay to discuss a stock lending scheme and a report on short sales.
Short selling is the sale of shares which are not held, in anticipation of a fall in prices.

Analysts in Bombay said earlier this week that among steps to reinvigorate the market, they were expecting companies to be allowed to buy back their shares. The market was also expecting taxes on shareholders' dividends to be scrapped, they said.

SEBI chairman D.R. Mehta met Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia, the highest ranking official in the Finance Ministry, in the capital New Delhi on Wednesday, prompting speculation that market-sensitive moves were in the offing.
The government spokesman said steps had already been announced to ensure continued high economic growth.
He cited the creation of a commission to supervise the sale of partial stakes in state-controlled firms as well as a telecommunications regulatory agency.
The spokesman said initial estimates of growth in India's gross domestic product (GDP) in the 1996/97 fiscal year ending on March 31 are "very, very encouraging".
He declined to disclose the official GDP growth estimate for 1996/97. In 1995/96, real GDP, adjusted for inflation, rose by 7.1 percent after 7.2 percent a year earlier.
